summary: Defines LDP, the Label Distribution Protocol, which lets MPLS routers tell each other which labels they have assigned to which traffic. Without this agreement, labels would have no shared meaning. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 5036.

eli5.summary: For tags to work, neighbors must agree on what each tag means. LDP is how they tell each other. A newer document later replaced it.

questions: how do mpls routers exchange labels
how does an ldp session start
subtitle: How MPLS routers tell their neighbors what each label means, so traffic can be switched along normal routed paths.

tldr.problem: In MPLS, two Label Switching Routers (LSRs) must agree on the meaning of the labels used to forward traffic between them. Without a shared understanding a label is meaningless.
tldr.mechanism: LDP finds neighbors with UDP Hello messages, opens a TCP session with each, and then exchanges messages that bind labels to Forwarding Equivalence Classes (FECs), building Label Switched Paths along normally routed paths.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3036 was a Standards Track specification of LDP. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 5036.

today: RFC 3036 was a Proposed Standard but has been obsoleted by RFC 5036, which is the current specification of LDP. Read RFC 5036 for the up-to-date text.

sections.title: What LDP Does
sections.content:
The MPLS architecture (RFC 3031) defines a label distribution protocol as the set of procedures by which one LSR tells another what the labels mean. LDP is a new protocol defined for this purpose. It is the set of procedures and messages by which LSRs set up Label Switched Paths (LSPs) by mapping network-layer routing information directly to data-link layer switched paths. The paths can end at a directly attached neighbor or at a network egress node.

Each LSP is associated with a FEC, which says which packets map to that LSP. LSPs extend through the network as each LSR joins its incoming label for a FEC to the outgoing label from the next hop. Two LSRs exchanging mappings are LDP peers with an LDP session between them, and the session is bi-directional.

There are four categories of message: discovery, session, advertisement and notification. LDP requires reliable, in-order delivery, so everything except discovery runs over TCP.
sections.eli5: LDP is the way neighbor routers tell each other what each sticker means, so a parcel can be passed along without opening it again at every stop.

sections.title: FECs, Label Spaces and Identifiers
sections.content:
A FEC is a set of one or more FEC elements. Two element types are defined: an Address Prefix (any length from 0 up to a full address) and a Host Address (a full host address). A packet is mapped to a Host Address match first; otherwise to the LSP with the longest matching prefix.

A label space is either per interface (for example ATM VCIs or Frame Relay DLCIs used as labels) or per platform. An LDP Identifier is six octets: the first four identify the LSR and must be globally unique, such as a 32-bit router Id, and the last two identify a label space within the LSR. For a platform-wide label space the last two octets are zero. An LSR advertising more than one label space to a peer uses a separate LDP session, and a separate TCP connection, for each.
sections.eli5: A FEC is a group of parcels that all travel the same way. A label space is the set of sticker numbers a router is allowed to hand out.

sections.title: Discovery and Session Setup
sections.content:
An LSR discovers peers by sending Hello messages as UDP packets to port 646. Link Hellos go to the all-routers-on-this-subnet multicast group for directly connected neighbors. Targeted Hellos go to a specific address, for peers that are not directly connected. Receiving a Hello creates a Hello adjacency, which is kept alive by a hold timer. The default hold time is 15 seconds for Link Hellos and 45 seconds for Targeted Hellos, and the interval between Hellos is recommended to be at most one third of the hold time.

To open a session, the LSR compares the transport addresses at the two ends as unsigned integers. The LSR with the higher address is active and connects to TCP port 646 on the other; the other is passive and waits. The active side sends an Initialization message to negotiate parameters such as protocol version, label distribution method and timer values. The passive side answers with its own Initialization and a KeepAlive. A session is operational once an LSR has received both an acceptable Initialization and a KeepAlive.

If Initialization messages keep being rejected, the retry must be delayed no less than 15 seconds, growing to a maximum of no less than 2 minutes. After setup, an LSR must send some LDP PDU at least every KeepAlive period, and sends a KeepAlive message when it has nothing else. A Shutdown message ends a session.
sections.eli5: Routers first shout hello on the local street. Once two have heard each other, the one with the bigger number makes the call, and they agree on the rules before swapping stickers.

sections.title: Label Distribution Modes
sections.content:
LDP supports three choices that shape how labels move:

  • Advertisement: in Downstream Unsolicited mode an LSR advertises labels without being asked; in Downstream on Demand mode it answers explicit requests. Each interface is set to one mode and the peers exchange modes at initialization.
  • Control: with independent control an LSR may advertise a mapping at any time; with ordered control it may do so only for a FEC it is the egress for, or one for which it already holds a mapping from the next hop.
  • Retention: conservative retention keeps only labels from the valid next hop, saving label space; liberal retention keeps every label received, so routing changes can be handled quickly at the cost of storing unneeded mappings.

LSRs also advertise their addresses with Address and Address Withdraw messages so that a peer's LDP Identifier can be mapped to next hop addresses. Optional loop detection uses Path Vector and Hop Count TLVs, and the TCP MD5 Signature Option can be configured to protect sessions.
sections.eli5: A router can hand out stickers only when asked or all the time, wait for the next stop's answer or not, and keep all stickers it is given or only the ones it needs.

sections.title: PDUs, TLVs and Messages
sections.content:
LDP messages travel in PDUs. Each PDU is a header followed by one or more messages; the messages need not be related. The header carries a 16-bit Version (this document specifies version 1), a PDU Length, and the six-octet LDP Identifier. Before negotiation completes, the maximum PDU length is 4096 bytes.

Most content is encoded as Type-Length-Value (TLV) objects. A TLV starts with a U bit and an F bit, then a 14-bit type and a 16-bit length. The U bit says whether an unknown TLV is silently ignored (set) or causes a notification and the whole message to be ignored (clear). The F bit says whether an unknown TLV is forwarded.

The messages cover the four categories. Label Mapping advertises a FEC-label binding, Label Request asks for one, Label Withdraw tells the peer to stop using one, Label Release says the sender no longer needs one, and Label Abort Request cancels an outstanding request. Notification messages carry a Status TLV and are either errors that end the session or advisory messages. Vendor-private and experimental ranges are reserved for extensions.
sections.eli5: Every note LDP sends has a header saying who sent it, then little labeled boxes inside. If a router sees a box it does not know, a flag says whether it can ignore it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo discusses spoofing, privacy and denial of service. For UDP discovery, spoofed Basic Hellos can be reduced by accepting them only on interfaces with trusted neighbors and ignoring Hellos not sent to the all-routers multicast group; Extended Hellos can be filtered with access lists. For TCP sessions, LDP specifies the TCP MD5 Signature Option for authenticity and integrity, and notes that RFC 2385 says MD5 is considered by some too weak, so a stronger digest could be adopted if defined.

LDP gives no privacy for label distribution. The memo argues privacy would not stop label spoofing because data packets carry labels in the clear. Like other TCP control protocols, LDP can face SYN attacks, and an LSR should avoid promiscuous TCP listens.
sections.eli5: LDP can lock its conversations with a shared password, but it does not hide them. The best protection is to talk only to routers you trust.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Protocol version; this specification defines version 1.

fields.name: PDU Length
fields.desc: Total PDU length in octets, excluding Version and PDU Length.

fields.name: LSR Id
fields.desc: First four octets of the LDP Identifier: a globally unique value, such as a 32-bit router Id.

fields.name: Label Space Id
fields.desc: Last two octets of the LDP Identifier; zero for a platform-wide label space.

items.label: Hello
items.desc: Discovery of potential peers, sent over UDP.

items.label: KeepAlive
items.desc: Monitors the integrity of the session.

items.label: Label Request
items.desc: Asks a peer for a label binding for a FEC.

items.label: Label Withdraw
items.desc: Tells the peer to stop using a binding.

items.label: Label Release
items.desc: Says the sender no longer needs a binding.
